title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We report a preregistered paired trial that measures whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single shared LLM generation per intent, deterministic verification, and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted verifier‑unsafe network changes relative to LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. Following preregistration (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N = 500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles using gpt-5-mini for generation and a deterministic network verifier for adjudication. Observed accepted final changes: baseline (LLM-only) 496/500; guarded (GVR) 500/500. Paired contingency: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The preregistered exact conditional two‑sided McNemar test on the discordant margin (n = 4, k = n10 = 4) yields p = 0.125. A predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates (one repair attempt per repaired task); total hosted model calls observed = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls), mean model calls per accepted change = 1.008. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the McNemar and bootstrap perspectives, document verifier semantics and known blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting semantics, present representative repaired‑episode diagnostics, and point readers to the archived evidence bundle and preregistration for machine‑readable artifacts.

sections.introduction:
High‑level intent translation into device configuration is a compelling automation target for network operations, but incorrect command sequences can cause outages. Large language models (LLMs) enable rapid intent‑to‑CLI translation but continue to produce hallucinations and factual errors that threaten operational safety. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a single canonical candidate with an LLM, deterministically verify it against explicit workflow, dependency, and availability rules, and when the verifier reports violations invoke a bounded repair attempt. This study asks whether a minimal GVR gate (one shared initial generation per intent, deterministic adjudication, and at most one automated repair) reduces verifier‑detected unsafe accepted changes relative to LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic workload.

We executed a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) with N = 500 distinct intents (paired baseline and guarded runs per intent) stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles. Our numerical findings are drawn verbatim from archived execution and analysis artifacts: baseline accepted = 496/500, guarded accepted = 500/500, paired discordants n10 = 4 (guarded success, baseline failure) and n01 = 0, producing an exact conditional McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 for the preregistered confirmatory test; a predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). We preserve the preregistration, frozen seeds, model configuration (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini), deterministic verifier semantics, and all execution artifacts. The remainder of the paper explains design choices, verifier capabilities and limitations, reconciles inferential perspectives, inspects repaired episodes, and discusses operational implications and validity threats.
sections.related_work:
Three strands of prior work underpin this study. First, multiple recent surveys and systems papers document rapid adoption of LLMs for intent translation, AIOps, and multi‑agent network management while repeatedly noting hallucination and factual errors as barriers to safe deployment; these sources motivate guardrail and verifier architectures [1,4,3]. Second, methodological proposals for tool‑augmented evaluate‑and‑repair pipelines emphasize paired trial designs, frozen preregistration, standardized validator semantics, and explicit accounting for orchestration costs (model calls and repairs); these blueprints informed our preregistered design and confirmatory estimator choice [2]. Third, deterministic and scalable network configuration verifiers have matured to enforce syntactic, workflow, dependency, and many availability properties; verifier scope varies with modeled vendor semantics and control‑plane fidelity and therefore with detectable hazards [5].

This experiment positions itself as a controlled, reproducible evaluation of a simple GVR gate using a canonical deterministic verifier rather than a claim of production readiness across heterogeneous vendor environments. It complements system papers that embed validation in multi‑agent frameworks by supplying artifact‑grounded paired evidence and explicit provider‑call accounting for a bounded repair policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and experimental design: The study was preregistered (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 distinct intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). Sampling seeds, the deterministic task generator, and analysis executor were frozen prior to execution. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar on discordant pairs; an exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was predeclared as descriptive.

Generation and orchestration: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model gpt-5-mini with fixed generation configuration. The baseline condition accepted that shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. In the guarded (GVR) condition the controller validated the shared candidate using a deterministic verifier and, if verification failed, issued at most one automated repair call to the same declared model. Provider accounting from the archived run records model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls); stage_counts record shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4. Mean hosted model calls per accepted change = 504/500 = 1.008; repaired pairs observed model calls per pair = 2 (shared initial + one repair).

Deterministic verifier semantics: The adjudicating verifier canonicalizes CLI sequences and enforces a rule set applied to the normalized commands. Its pipeline comprises: (i) syntactic parsing and canonical normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (patterns such as must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability and group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome. For each episode the verifier emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, a violation list and codes, and boolean valid. A human‑readable codebook maps violation codes to descriptions (archived with the run).

Repair policy and prompt semantics: When the verifier failed the shared_initial candidate the GVR controller issued a single constrained repair prompt to gpt-5-mini containing: (a) the abstracted intent, (b) short descriptions of verifier violation codes, and (c) an instruction to produce a corrected canonical CLI sequence. The repair candidate was accepted only if the verifier returned valid = true. All repair prompts, repair responses, and subsequent verifier traces for repaired episodes are archived and summarized in Results.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and primary counts: Execution completed the planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 1000; completed_pair_count = 500) with no failed episodes. Observed accepted‑change counts: baseline 496/500 (0.992), guarded 500/500 (1.000). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked in four episodes; each repair attempt produced a subsequent verifier PASS. Provider accounting: model_calls_used = 504 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 4).

Confirmatory inferential analysis (preregistered): The preregistered exact conditional McNemar conditions on the observed discordant margin n = n10 + n01 and evaluates a two‑sided binomial tail on k = n10 with p = 0.5. For n = 4 and k = 4 the one‑sided tail P(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16; doubling for two‑sided yields p = 0.125. Under the preregistered decision rule this p‑value does not meet the preregistered confirmatory threshold and we therefore do not claim confirmatory statistical significance.

Predeclared exploratory estimate: The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) equals [0.002, 0.016]. The bootstrap resampling does not condition on the observed discordant margin, so with only four discordants the percentile interval can exclude zero even while the conditional McNemar is not significant; we report this interval as predeclared exploratory descriptive evidence.

Repaired‑episode diagnostics (artifact‑grounded summaries): The four repaired/discordant pairs corresponded to verifier‑detectable sequencing or group/paired‑field dependency violations. Recorded verifier violation codes and descriptions (as archived) are:
- pair-000090 | [MUST_BE_DOWN_FOR_FIELD] — VLAN/field changed while interface remained admin up; required 'must be down' sequencing violated. repair_invoked: yes; model_calls_for_pair: 2; final_score: PASS.
- pair-000341 | [MAKE_BEFORE_BREAK] — Backup uplink not enabled before primary was shut; violates 'make‑before‑break' availability rule. repair_invoked: yes; model_calls_for_pair: 2; final_score: PASS.
- pair-000381 | [PAIRED_MTU_CHANGE] — MTU changed on one side of a paired link without coordinating the paired interface's MTU change. repair_invoked: yes; model_calls_for_pair: 2; final_score: PASS.
- pair-000413 | [GROUP_AVAILABILITY_CONSTRAINT] — Both edge interfaces placed admin down simultaneously, violating minimum_active_in_groups constraint. repair_invoked: yes; model_calls_for_pair: 2; final_score: PASS.

Representative per‑episode validator traces, normalized configurations, repair prompts/responses and verifier violation lists are archived in the evidence bundle. All numerical totals and contingency counts above are taken directly from archived analysis outputs.
sections.discussion:
Reconciling McNemar and bootstrap perspectives: The GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted; these four are the only discordants (n = 4). The preregistered exact conditional McNemar conditions on n and assesses whether the direction of discordance is unlikely under exchangeability; with n = 4 the two‑sided p = 0.125, which does not cross the preregistered significance threshold. The predeclared bootstrap CI excludes zero ([0.002, 0.016]) because resampling paired observations without conditioning on margins can repeatedly include the same small set of favorable discordants; therefore the bootstrap provides an informative effect‑size description but has reduced frequentist coverage guarantees under very small discordant counts. We adhere to the preregistered McNemar decision for our primary confirmatory claim and present the bootstrap interval as predeclared exploratory evidence.

Design rationale and practical interpretation: We selected a conservative GVR gate (single shared initial generation per intent; deterministic verifier as the adjudicator; at most one repair) to isolate the marginal impact of a low‑latency verifier plus a bounded repair loop while keeping orchestration cost low. In this synthetic workload the baseline was near ceiling (496/500); the preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08, so realized power fell short because only four discordant pairs occurred. Operationally, the observed 4 repairs (0.8% repair invocation rate) produced modest extra model calls (total = 504), suggesting that, for workloads with low baseline unsafe‑proposal rates, a compact deterministic verifier plus single repair can intercept verifier‑detectable hazards at low orchestration cost. However, realized operational benefit will depend on baseline failure rates, verifier fidelity, adversarial intent distributions, and latency constraints of higher‑fidelity verifiers.

Verifier scope, blind spots, and safety implications: The verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state—adequate to detect the four repaired episodes in this run. Importantly, verifier PASS is necessary for the experiment’s safety definition but not sufficient for full production safety: the verifier intentionally omits vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing and convergence models, session/execution errors, hardware resource limits, and other runtime side effects. Therefore production automation demands expanded verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, and telemetry‑driven checks) and staged rollout with human‑in‑the‑loop validation.

Threats to validity and generality: Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, deterministic seeds, frozen task generation and complete execution accounting (complete_pair_count = 500; failed_episode_count = 0). Construct validity is limited by synthetic device templates and an intentionally scoped verifier: encoded workflow policies match the synthetic intent grammar but imperfectly model vendor behavior and dynamic control‑plane hazards. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication and vendor‑specific parsing remain future work. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan expected a larger paired difference, but near‑ceiling baseline performance yielded only four discordants and limited confirmatory sensitivity. These limitations explain the observed pattern—a small numerical paired difference that is descriptively bounded away from zero by bootstrap resampling but not confirmatorily significant under the preregistered McNemar rule.

Operational implications and future steps: A lightweight deterministic verifier acting as a pre‑execution gate can prevent verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals at modest model‑call cost when baseline LLM performance is already high. To move toward production, automation systems should (a) expand verifier fidelity to include vendor semantics and control‑plane simulation, (b) quantify latencies and computational costs of higher‑fidelity verifiers at inventory scale, (c) evaluate GVR under adversarial or domain‑shifted intents, and (d) replicate across models and templated automation comparators (the preregistered templated‑automation arm was not executed in this run).
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference estimate = 0.008 produced an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016] while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification combined with a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in the studied synthetic setting, but broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated‑automation comparator which was not executed in this run. All execution and analysis artifacts, the preregistration, per‑episode verifier traces, provider accounting, and analysis logs are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29).

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. The generation model used in the archived run was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration). Key automated components in the run were a deterministic task generator, a deterministic network verifier, and a GVR controller implementing shared_initial_generation plus at most one automated repair per task. The study was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here are: N = 500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The immutable initial master prompt for this run is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt) and its SHA‑256 is 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and this revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this archived run; therefore the original preregistered multiplicity plan that would have adjusted for two confirmatory tests was not applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to the deterministic verifier’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation across two planned tests is not applicable to the present execution.
